name: Pritikin diet

card.summary: The Pritikin diet is a very-low-fat, high-fibre, minimally processed way of eating, paired with exercise, that people use to lose weight and lean out.
card.note: Reviews note possible insufficient fat and mineral losses from high fibre intake.

quick.overview:
The Pritikin diet is built around whole, unprocessed foods that are low in fat and high in fibre, and it is part of a wider Pritikin Program that includes exercise. Its appearance payoff is weight and body-fat loss, which shows as a leaner face and body.

Studies of the Pritikin Program, mostly in residential or supervised settings, report reductions in body weight or BMI alongside improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar. A 1995 assessment described it as nutritionally adequate but noted that its low fat content can make compliance difficult.
quick.how: People eat mainly vegetables, fruit, whole grains and legumes, limiting red meat, alcohol and processed foods, and combine this with regular exercise. In research settings the programs run from a few weeks (12 to 26 days in some studies) to six weeks.
quick.risks: Reviews have flagged possible insufficient fat intake and mineral losses from very high fibre. Critics in the literature describe it as hard to stick with. People on medication for blood pressure or diabetes are generally advised by clinicians to involve a doctor when changing diet.

lead: The Pritikin diet is a low-fat, high-fibre eating plan that limits red meat, alcohol and processed foods; it is part of a lifestyle regimen created by Nathan Pritikin that also includes exercise.[3] A book on the diet became a best-seller in 1979.[3]

For appearance, its route is weight and body-fat reduction: the very-low-fat, high-fibre pattern was designed to be filling at low calorie density, and studies report weight or BMI declines alongside improved heart-disease risk markers.[4][5]
It was considered radical at launch, but Wikipedia notes its core precepts now largely resemble mainstream nutrition advice, while also categorising it as a fad diet.[3]

chain: Eat unprocessed, low-fat, high-fibre foods with exercise
Lower calorie density and body weight
angle.text: The diet and its accompanying exercise reduce weight and body fat in studies, which shows up as a slimmer face and physique. Skin and general health claims come from the broader cardiometabolic improvements.

infobox: Very low fat, high fibre, low sodium

paras: The diet emphasises whole, minimally processed foods and limits red meat, alcohol and processed items.[3] The Pritikin Program combines it with low sodium and exercise.[4][6]

Nathan Pritikin's program became widely known after a 1979 best-selling book.[3] Consumer Reports published a critical assessment in 1982, and the New York Times covered those who had used the diet against heart disease in 1985.[3]

A 1995 paper by Alpers and colleagues called it nutritionally adequate but said its low fat content made it unpalatable, so compliance is likely low.[3] A 1991 summary noted possible insufficient fat and mineral losses from high fibre.[7] A 1984 survey of popular diets recommended against several including Pritikin for specified reasons.[8]

A study of 67 people with metabolic syndrome who attended 12 to 15 days at the Pritikin Longevity Center reported BMI down 3%, blood pressure, glucose and LDL cholesterol down 10 to 15%, and triglycerides down 36%, with HDL cholesterol down 3%.[1]

A 6-week randomised trial in 54 people with overweight or obesity found weight down 5.0% versus 0.5% with standard care, with improvements in HbA1c and cholesterol.[2] A 26-day Brazilian study of 20 patients reported lower blood pressure and improved cardiac measures.[5]

timeline.event: Consumer Reports article on claims versus facts.[3]
